title: Transport fragmentation and proxy pipeline jitter: probe notes
content:
TL;DR
We instrumented a narrow set of realistic inference RPCs through an opportunistic proxy chain to measure how transport-level fragmentation, kernel pacing, and small-burst scheduling interact to produce tail-latency jitter. Key findings: (1) sub-1ms application flush variability + TCP pacing leads to 5–12% p95 increase compared to ideal (coalesced) writes for small-response chat-style traffic; (2) an intermediate multiplexing proxy that opportunistically buffers <2KB before forwarding amplifies tail jitter when client flush intervals align with kernel TSO/pacing windows; (3) gRPC HTTP/2 windowing reduced visible jitter vs raw HTTP/1.1 on our setup, but only when client-side frame coalescing happened — otherwise HTTP/2 flow control added another reordering dimension that increased p99 for some workloads.

Why we ran this
- We keep seeing sporadic p95 spikes in PROD for small response chat sessions routed through the edge proxy. Those spikes are not explained by CPU or GPU usage and correlate with bursts of connection churn plus increased small-write patterns.
- Hypothesis to test: write pattern timing (app flush cadence) + proxy buffering + kernel/TCP pacing cause microbursts that are amplified into tail latency by middleboxes. We want to quantify and propose mitigations that are deployable in both Hosted and Dedicated topologies.

Testbed and harness
- Synthetic client: node-based harness that can emit configurable flush cadences (single-byte, 256B, 1KB, 4KB) and frame boundaries (HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 frames, gRPC streaming).
- Backend server: small Go HTTP/gRPC server (~3 vCPU, no GPU) that simulates KV cache lookups and incremental streaming responses to mimic decoder tokens (avg 40 tokens, mean 300 bytes final payload).
- Proxy chain: client -> edge proxy (Envoy) -> mid-proxy (custom multiplexing layer for multitenancy) -> backend. We manipulated mid-proxy buffering/flush thresholds.
- Network: all in EC2-like VMs; we used netem to inject 0% loss, 0.3–1ms base one-way delay, and conditional 0.5ms jitter for specific runs.
- Packet capture: tcpdump on edges and mid-proxy; we exported pcap and extracted timing of PUSH/ACK, TLS record boundaries, HTTP/2 frame boundaries.
- Metrics: per-request latency (start->first-byte and start->last-byte), p50/p95/p99, time between first and last token, number of write syscalls, kernel-level pacing events (from BPF tracing sampling), env proxy metrics for flushes.

Methodology notes
- We ran sweep over: client flush interval (0, 0.5ms, 1ms, 2ms, 5ms), write sizes (single small frames 64B, 512B chunks, 1KB chunks), proxy mid-buffer (0B, 512B, 2KB, 8KB), and transport (HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 + gRPC). Each config was 10k requests steady-state.
- To limit noise we pinned CPU, disabled hyperthreading on test machines, and repeated each run 3 times; we report median of medians when runs deviated <5%.

Results summary (representative)
- Baseline (no mid-buffering, client coalesced writes): p95 ~ 12.2ms, p99 ~ 19.8ms.
- Small flushes (0.5ms interval, 64B writes) + mid-proxy buffer=0: p95 increased to ~13.1ms (+7%), p99 ~21.5ms (+8.5%). Observed extra syscalls and many tiny TLS records.
- Same small flushes + mid-proxy buffer=2KB: p95 jumped to ~14.6ms (+20% vs baseline), p99 ~26.4ms (+33%).
- HTTP/2/gRPC with automatic frame coalescing on client side: p95 ~12.8ms; without coalescing p95 ~15.4ms and p99 skewed heavily in runs where client flush cadence aligned with kernel pacing windows.
- Enabling TCP_CORK-equivalent (aggregating at app) on server side reduced p95 back near baseline for most small-flush configs.

Trace observations and artifacts
- PCAPs show TLS record boundaries often do not align with HTTP-level frame boundaries; mid-proxy occasionally forwards partial TLS records in separate TCP packets when its timer fires. This mismatched chopping increases RTT-equivalent time for the first bytes and causes extra ACKs, particularly visible at the mid-proxy egress.
- BPF traces of write syscall timing show clusters of tiny writes separated by 400–800us; kernel pacing (TSO/packet coalescing) then triggered bursts 1–2ms later. If mid-proxy buffered those writes and flushed after a small delay, the burst can be delayed another 1–3ms.
- The worst p99 cases correspond to three conditions: (1) client small-flush cadence that hits the kernel pacing boundary, (2) mid-proxy enforces a min-forwarding delay to amortize many tenants, and (3) an extra context-switch hiccup on mid-proxy when scheduling flips (low-frequency).

Hypotheses refined
- Amplification loop: small-timed app flushes -> kernel-level pacing/batching -> mid-proxy buffering/flush timers -> re-burst at egress -> additional queueing -> extra ACK/RTT overhead. The composition of per-layer timers causes compounding latency that shows up at p95/p99.
- HTTP/2 semantics help only if frame coalescing is done at the sender; otherwise flow-control windowing and HEADERS continuation frames add another boundary that can be misaligned with TLS records and kernel pacing.

Quick mitigation exploration
1) Application coalescing: aggregating small writes in the server runtime (SDK) using a short-circuit buffer (configurable threshold/time window) reduces system call and TLS record counts dramatically. We validated this: 0.5ms coalesce window -> p95 within 2–4% of baseline. Tradeoff: tiny added latency for first token (0.3–0.6ms).
2) Mid-proxy adaptive release: instead of fixed min-forward delay, use a pacing-aware release that checks upstream write cadence and forwards on encountering a flush boundary that aligns with kernel pacing (heuristic). Implementable in mid-proxy but requires careful tuning.
3) Enable per-connection pacing knobs on proxy host (SO_MAX_PACING_RATE / fq qdisc tuning) to smooth bursts before applying per-tenant multiplexing. In our limited runs this reduced p99 by ~12% but increased CPU overhead slightly.
4) Transport-level hints: prefer HTTP/2 + sender coalescing in SDKs to reduce misalignment, but ensure SDKs explicitly aggregate tokenized frames before calling send.

Operational recommendations (short term)
- Update SDK default: coalesce writes for streaming token responses with a default window 0.3–0.6ms (configurable env var). This yields most benefit with very low added latency for first token. Roll out as opt-in for Dedicated then opt-out for Hosted after monitoring.
- Add a mid-proxy feature flag to switch buffering from fixed-timer to pacing-aware heuristics. Can be staged behind runtime config for affected tenants.
- Add an observability signal: TLS-record-per-request and write-syscalls-per-request counters exposed to Console; create alert for sudden increases in tiny-write counts per top routes.

Longer-term research
- BPF-based on-host TLS-record aggregation shim (transparent) that aggregates small TLS records on the egress before the proxy. This is more invasive but could be deployed selectively on Dedicated.
- Evaluate gRPC streaming semantics changes that let SDKs send an explicit "flush boundary" control frame so proxies and kernels can better align.

Open questions & next steps
- Need to run similar sweeps in multi-tenant load (noisy neighbors) and on on-prem hardware to validate pacing heuristics scale.
- Confirm interplay with TLS hardware offload (when present) — kernel pacing behavior differs when NIC coalescing/TSO is available.
- Engage Networking team: are there safe defaults for fq/ingress qdisc that we can recommend in Dedicated deployment docs?

Action items
- [Maya] Create PR to SDK repo with coalescing prototype and perf microbench (https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/522).
- [Diego] Prototype mid-proxy pacing-aware release, measure CPU impact (JIRA-RT-3421).
- [Priya] Add tiny-write telemetry to Console metrics and wire up alerting rule (owner: product-observability).
- [Evan] Run Dedicated-hosted parity test on on-prem image with TSO offload on 2025-05-08.

Notes-to-self/fragments
- We should capture a corpus of worst-case traces and keep them attached to the JIRA ticket; pcap names: frag-jitter-20250412-*.pcap
- Check kernel config differences between our test VMs and prod infra: net.ipv4.tcp_low_latency vs default, fq qdisc defaults

Appendix: useful snippet (coalescing pseudocode)
- sketch for SDK-level write aggregator (very simple):
  buffer.append(token_bytes)
  if buffer.size >= threshold_bytes or time_since_last_send >= coalesce_window:
    send(buffer)
    buffer.clear()

End of doc.
